reasons: [alternatives_counterarguments/major] D1 [verdict ('moderate at best'); alternatives 'Defer until the freeze ends'; counterarguments; criteriaAssessments C5] The draft argues one side of the second half of the decision objective (does the impact justify an exception at all?). The verdict says 'The case for an exception is moderate at best', and the Defer alternative cites 'low staffing' as a reason against deploying the retry. The same holiday staffing problem also weakens the manual workaround: finance staff are on leave, and manual handling of more than EUR 10k refunds carries a higher error risk. The draft never raises this. The counterarguments section also leaves out the strongest case for an exception: customers waiting on delayed high-value refunds, possible contractual, scheme or regulatory deadlines for refunds, and the reputational cost. Of the four counterarguments listed, none argues for an exception on impact grounds. The draft therefore downgrades the exception case without weighing the best evidence for it.

[reasoning_validity/major] D1 [verdict ('These limits govern when a refund is completed, not how it is processed'); C5 assessment and strengths ('Refund time limits govern completion, not method'); CL13; counterarguments item 5 response] The new synthesis that holds up the pro-exception analysis says external refund limits 'govern when a refund is completed, not how it is processed', so 'a manual workaround completed on time meets them'. The draft's own evidence contradicts this. E13 (CRD Art. 13) requires reimbursement 'using the same means of payment as the original transaction unless the consumer expressly agrees otherwise', and C5 itself says 'the trader must refund within 14 days by the same means of payment'. Card-scheme credit rules (E14, E16, E17) also assume the credit goes back to the original card. The workaround uses a 'back-office tool' whose payment rail is unknown (E22, E14 limitations note it may be bank transfer). So the workaround may break the 'how' requirement even when finance keeps pace. The conditional 'moderate if finance can keep pace' therefore understates a possible compliance problem with the workaround itself, which is the one condition the draft says decides the exception case. This is new material in draft-2.
